pathophysiology.summary: Hypoglycaemia is the commonest acute complication of insulin and sulfonylurea treatment. When glucose falls, adrenergic warning symptoms come first; if glucose keeps falling the brain is starved of glucose (neuroglycopenia), causing confusion, seizures and coma.
keyMechanisms: Too much insulin effect relative to glucose supply: missed meals or fasting, exercise, weight loss, or reduced insulin clearance in kidney failure.
Adrenergic phase (autonomic): palpitations, sweating, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia, tingling, hunger.
Neuroglycopenic phase: dizziness, headache, blurred vision, poor concentration, behaviour change or aggression, confusion, seizures, coma.
Hypoglycaemia unawareness: repeated episodes blunt the adrenergic response, so warning symptoms are lost; risk of severe hypoglycaemia rises six-fold.
Long-acting sulfonylureas (e.g. glibenclamide) keep stimulating insulin release, so hypoglycaemia recurs for 24–48 h.

symptoms: Adrenergic: palpitations, sweating, anxiety, tremor, hunger.
Neuroglycopenic: headache, blurred vision, confusion, behaviour change, aggression, fatigue.
physicalSigns: Reduced GCS or abnormal behaviour; may mimic stroke or intoxication.
Look for injection sites, medical ID bracelet, signs of infection or kidney disease.
redFlags: Unconscious or unable to swallow: IV dextrose or IM glucagon now; do not give oral glucose
Seizures, deteriorating consciousness, or persistent vomiting (MOH call-the-doctor criteria)
Severe hypoglycaemia can cause arrhythmias, QT prolongation, hypokalaemia, MI and stroke: ECG and monitor
Hypoglycaemia on a long-acting sulfonylurea: recurrence for 24–48 h; admit and observe
Recurrent hypoglycaemia despite treatment, or hypoglycaemia without diabetes treatment: look for another cause
precipitants: Prior severe hypoglycaemia; HbA1c below 6.0%; long insulin duration; autonomic neuropathy; elderly; cognitive impairment; pregnancy.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Focal deficit persists after glucose is corrected. Always check glucose in any acute neurological presentation.
History and toxicology; check glucose because intoxication and hypoglycaemia can coexist.
Glucose normal at the time of the event.

differentials.condition: Spontaneous (non-drug) hypoglycaemia: sepsis, organ failure (especially liver failure, end-stage kidney disease), cancer, dementia
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: No insulin or sulfonylurea to explain it, or recurrence after dextrose; carries a higher mortality than drug-induced hypoglycaemia and needs work-up.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Immediately; then 5 min after IV dextrose, 15 min after oral glucose or glucagon
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Level 1: below 3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL). Level 2: below 3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dL). Level 3: severe event needing another person's help, at any value.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Treat until glucose is above 4.0 mmol/L. Send a laboratory sample but do not wait for the result.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess ABC, consciousness and ability to swallow
actions: Check capillary glucose and send a laboratory sample; do not wait for the result.

clinicalManagement.title: Conscious and able to drink
actions: 15 g fast glucose: half a cup of apple or orange juice, or one tablespoon of sugar dissolved in water, or one tablespoon of honey.
Recheck glucose after 15 min; if still 4.0 mmol/L or less, repeat (up to 3 times) until above 4.0.
Then give a 15–20 g complex carbohydrate snack (e.g. one toast).

clinicalManagement.title: Unconscious or unable to drink
actions: IV access secured: give 50% dextrose and recheck glucose after 5 min; repeat the same dose until above 4.0 mmol/L.
No IV access: glucagon 1 mg SC or IM; recheck after 15 min; repeat if still 4.0 or less.
When awake and able to eat: a meal with 30 g complex carbohydrate (2–3 toasts).
25 mL of 50% dextrose IV over 1–3 min.
50 mL of 50% dextrose IV over 1–3 min.

clinicalManagement.title: Find the cause and adjust treatment
actions: Identify precipitants (missed meal, exercise, dose error, kidney failure, infection, alcohol).
Adjust insulin or other glucose-lowering drugs; avoid high-risk agents in recurrent hypoglycaemia.
Long-acting sulfonylurea (e.g. glibenclamide, gliclazide MR): observe for 24–48 h.
Unexplained hypoglycaemia on insulin or oral agents: reduce the dose by 10–25% (MOH).
Hypoglycaemia unawareness or level 2 on insulin: relax glycaemic targets for at least 1 month (up to 3 months).

regimens.frequency: Repeat every 15 min until glucose above 4.0 (up to 3 times)
adjustments: Not if unable to swallow safely

regimens.indication: Unconscious or unable to swallow, IV access
regimens.dose: 25 mL if glucose 2.5–4.0; 50 mL if below 2.5
adjustments: Recheck glucose before each repeat dose

regimens.frequency: Repeat after 15 min if glucose still 4.0 or less
adjustments: Prescribe to all insulin-treated patients at risk

patientEducation: Recognise early symptoms; carry glucose; medical ID bracelet.
Driving: keep glucose in the car; check before and during long journeys.
Ramadan fasting: break the fast if glucose is below 3.9 mmol/L.
lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
dischargeCriteria: Fully alert, eating, glucose stable above 4.0 mmol/L.
Cause identified; not on a long-acting sulfonylurea (or observed 24–48 h).
A responsible adult can monitor at home; glucagon prescribed for those at risk.
